'''Amr ibn Dinar''' ({{Langx|ar|عمرو بن دينار|translit=ʿAmr ibn Dīnār}}, {{Circa|46-126 AH/666-744 CE}}) was a seventh-century Muslim [[faqīh|jurist]] and [[hadith]] transmitter from the ''[[tabi'un]]'' who served as the [[mufti]] of [[Mecca]].

== Biography ==
Amr ibn Dinar's exact date of birth is unknown, but Islamic biographical dictionaries estimate it to be around {{Circa|{{AH|46}}}}.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|last=Motzki|first=Harald|title=The Origins of Islamic Jurisprudence: Meccan Fiqh Before the Classical Schools|publisher=Brill|year=2002|isbn=9789004121317|location=|pages=262–268}}</ref> He was a ''[[mawla]]'' of either [[Madhhaj|Banu Maddhij]] or the [[Banu Jumah]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last=Motzki|first=Harald|date=2009-10-01|title=ʿAmr b. Dīnār|url=https://referenceworks.brillonline.com/entries/encyclopaedia-of-islam-3/amr-b-dinar-COM_22955|journal=Encyclopaedia of Islam, THREE|language=en}}</ref> In his early years, he attended the study circles of [[Ibn Abbas]]' students, possibly in Mecca and [[Ta'if]].<ref name=":0" /> He later studied under [[Ata ibn Abi Rabah]] and [[Tawus ibn Kaysan]] and was regarded positively, the latter encouraging his son to study under him.<ref name=":1" />

He gained renown as a scholar by the beginning of the eighth century and was offered the position of ''mufti'' of Mecca by the [[Umayyad Caliphate|Umayyads]] after the death of Ata. Although he initially refused, he accepted after being offered the post a second time following the death of Ata's successor, [[Qays ibn Sa'd]].<ref name=":0" /> Amr's most prominent student was [[Sufyan ibn ʽUyaynah]], through whom much of his biographical information is transmitted.<ref name=":0" />

Biographical works suggest he possessed an odd personality: he seemingly arbitrarily refused to answer questioners, required his students to carry him in and out of mosques and expressed his displeasure by weeping and pretending to be blind.<ref name=":0" /> He was opposed to his students recording his opinions on the grounds that they were subject to change.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Uzunpostalci|first=Mustafa|date=|title=AMR b. DÎNÂR - TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi|url=https://islamansiklopedisi.org.tr/amr-b-dinar|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200925030233/https://islamansiklopedisi.org.tr/amr-b-dinar |archive-date=2020-09-25 |access-date=2020-08-22|website=islamansiklopedisi.org.tr|language=en}}</ref> He also disapproved of them writing down hadith narrated through him, although several, including Ibn Uyaynah, transmitted hadith from him in written form regardless.<ref>{{Cite book|last=al-Azami|first=Muhammad Mustafa|title=Studies in Early Hadith Literature: with a critical edition of some early texts|publisher=American Trust Publications|year=1978|isbn=|location=Indiapolis, Indiana|pages=21, 79}}</ref>

Amr died around {{Circa|{{AH|126}}}} and was succeeded as ''mufti'' by his peer [[Ibn Abi Najih]].<ref name=":0" />
